card.description: A rectangular grid code that makes Shor's two repetition protections local by treating nearest-neighbour XX and ZZ parities as gauge generators. These gauge measurements need not commute with one another: only their center fixes the protected subspace. The unconstrained gauge subsystem absorbs local changes of representative, while one row-spanning X string and one column-spanning Z string carry the logical qubit.

views.description: Vertical XX pairs and horizontal ZZ pairs generate a nonabelian gauge group. Multiplying every vertical pair across two neighboring rows gives an X stabilizer; multiplying every horizontal pair across two neighboring columns gives a Z stabilizer. The constructor verifies that these center generators commute with the full gauge group and lie in its span.

Perfect gauge readout reduces the two Pauli channels to classical repetition inference in perpendicular directions. A bare logical X may be placed on any complete row and a bare logical Z on any complete column; parallel representatives differ only by gauge action. The engine constructs the protected quotient C(S)/G, exactly enumerates the three shipped finite instances, and independently validates any seeded upper-bound witness. Scalable lower bounds and presentation-equivalence certificates remain open under wanted/subsystem-dressed-distance.

origin.converter: qeclib.gf2.rank + Bacon–Shor gauge-span and logical-pair checks

views.description: Reading the same XX/ZZ links as Hamiltonian terms produces the square quantum-compass pattern and its rigid line symmetries. This dictionary does not turn the ordinary static Bacon–Shor model into a topological or self-correcting memory; locality belongs to the gauge generators, while the stabilizer products grow with a linear dimension.

A surface-code tensor network can be reorganized by declaring selected dangling legs logical rather than physical. The reassignment exposes the Bacon–Shor weight-two gauge structure and explains the relationship as a change of subsystem bookkeeping, not an equality of stabilizer tables.

The gauge-term anticommutation graph records which perpendicular XX and ZZ links meet once. It is a useful contrast with free-fermion subsystem constructions, but the ordinary Bacon–Shor compass Hamiltonian itself is not labeled free-fermion solvable: the fetched source explicitly treats it as the obstructed relative as of 2026-08-02.

Floquet–Bacon–Shor replaces the static gauge-center object with a period-four measurement schedule whose detectors and logical representatives evolve in time. Its superconducting logical-operation demonstration is therefore evidence for a dynamical descendant, not a hardware realization of this card's static check matrix.

params.rows: Number of physical-qubit rows; at least two.
params.columns: Number of physical-qubit columns; at least two.

decoders.noise: finite rectangular blocks with perfect two-qubit gauge outcomes under stochastic Pauli noise

decoders.notes: Here the input includes a protocol-specific history of gauge outcomes, flags, or encoded-ancilla checks. realizations.description: A nine-data-qubit Bacon–Shor logical block with four ancillas demonstrated fault-tolerant preparation, measurement, corrected rotations, and stabilizer extraction. This is a fixed-distance primitive suite, not an increasing-distance below-threshold memory experiment.

Highly rectangular blocks are combined with teleportation and biased elementary operations so geometry protects the dominant Pauli channel. The resource claim includes ancilla preparation, verification, and correction; it is not supplied by block aspect ratio alone.

relations.how: For the square three-by-three member in this constructor's orientation, promote all horizontal ZZ gauge pairs to stabilizers. intuition:
# Bacon–Shor code

## Essence

**The object.** Put one qubit at every site of a `rows × columns` rectangle,
using row-major labels `q(r,c)`. Generate a subsystem gauge group from

- `XX` on every vertical nearest-neighbour pair, and
- `ZZ` on every horizontal nearest-neighbour pair.

A vertical `XX` and a horizontal `ZZ` that meet at one site anticommute. That
is not a defect: gauge generators are allowed to disturb an unprotected gauge
subsystem. The protected codespace is fixed only by the commuting center of
the gauge group. Multiplying all vertical `XX` links across one gap between
rows produces an X-type center strip; multiplying all horizontal `ZZ` links
across one gap between columns produces a Z-type center strip. The
[gauge-center derivation](pedagogy/gauge-center-and-qubits.md) proves their
centrality and counts every protected and gauge degree of freedom.

For an `r × c` rectangle the formal ledger is

`n = rc`, `k = 1`, `gauge qubits = (r-1)(c-1)`,
`d_X = c`, `d_Z = r`, and `d = min(r,c)`.

Here `d_X` names the lightest X-type dressed logical and `d_Z` the lightest
Z-type dressed logical in the entry's Pauli convention. The shared Atlas
referee now constructs `C(S)/G`, enumerates complete Pauli-weight layers, and
recomputes the total dressed distance of every shipped finite instance. Those
three `d` claims are therefore `verified`. The named sector formulas remain
literature-attributed because the shared API does not separately certify
`d_X` and `d_Z`. Beyond the exact-search ceiling, a seeded search may establish
an achieved upper bound only; scalable lower bounds and equivalence-safe
presentation changes remain on the
[subsystem dressed-distance gap](../../wanted.html#subsystem-dressed-distance).

**The trick.** Bacon–Shor does not make Shor's long repetition constraints
disappear. It factorizes each long center measurement into local weight-two
gauge measurements whose outcomes can be multiplied afterward. Locality is
gained at the measurement interface; the stabilizers in the center still
span complete two-row or two-column strips.

**One sentence.** Bacon–Shor protects one qubit by reducing X and Z errors,
modulo local gauge motion, to two perpendicular classical repetition
problems.

## Design problem

Shor's nested repetition code has a clean decoding story, but some of its
stabilizer checks cover two complete length-`c` or length-`r` blocks. Directly
coupling an ancilla to such a growing support invites correlated faults and a
large circuit. The subsystem move asks a sharper question:

> Which local observables contain the same protected syndrome if we agree not
> to preserve every degree of freedom inside the encoded block?

The answer is the pair-gauge grammar above. Individual gauge outcomes are not
simultaneous eigenvalues because perpendicular links can anticommute. Only
products in the center define persistent stabilizer syndromes. An error and
that error multiplied by a gauge operator act identically on the protected
logical qubit, so recovery only needs the correct gauge coset.

This trade has four costs that the word "local" can hide:

- the center stabilizers remain long strips even though their measured factors
  have weight two;
- X- and Z-type gauge measurements must be ordered, repeated, or embedded in
  a circuit whose time history is part of the decoder input;
- the disposable subsystem grows as `(r-1)(c-1)`, so `n-rank(S)` is not the
  protected logical-qubit count;
- a decoder, threshold, or logical operation belongs to a specified
  extraction protocol and noise model, not to the static rectangle alone.

The [measurement and fault-tolerance ledger](pedagogy/measurement-and-fault-tolerance.md)
keeps perfect gauge readout, repeated circuits, encoded-ancilla extraction,
self-concatenated surgery, and the Floquet descendant separate.

## Derivation chain

**1. Fix the orientation.** Qubits are ordered by rows. X-type gauge edges are
vertical and Z-type gauge edges are horizontal. Transposing the rectangle and
swapping X with Z gives an equivalent convention, but formulas such as
`d_X=c` and `d_Z=r` depend on declaring this orientation first.

**2. Multiply local edges into center strips.** For a fixed gap between rows,
multiply its `c` vertical `XX` edges. Interior cancellations do not occur;
instead the product is X on every qubit in the two adjacent rows. Any
horizontal `ZZ` gauge edge meets that strip on zero or two sites, so it
commutes. The perpendicular construction gives a Z strip over two adjacent
columns. Thus all `r-1+c-1` strips commute with the entire gauge group.

**3. Count the quotient.** There are `c(r-1)` independent X gauge rows and
`r(c-1)` independent Z gauge rows. Their symplectic supports occupy different
halves of the binary matrix, so

`rank(G) = c(r-1) + r(c-1) = 2rc-r-c`.

The center basis has rank `rank(S)=r+c-2`. The subsystem identities

`k = n - (rank(G)+rank(S))/2`

and

`g = (rank(G)-rank(S))/2`

give one protected qubit and `(r-1)(c-1)` gauge qubits. The
[rank ledger](pedagogy/gauge-center-and-qubits.md) derives these formulas from
open-chain incidence matrices rather than assuming the generators are
independent.

**4. Find bare logicals.** X on one complete row commutes with every gauge
generator: each horizontal Z edge overlaps it twice. Z on one complete column
commutes for the perpendicular reason. The two strings cross once and
anticommute. Moving to a parallel row or column multiplies by a center strip,
which is itself in the gauge group, so the protected action is unchanged.

**5. Dress and reduce.** Multiplying an X logical by vertical X gauge edges can
move its one X within each column independently. What survives gauge motion is
the parity in every column. A nontrivial X logical has odd parity in all `c`
columns, so it needs at least one occupied site per column and has weight at
least `c`. A row realizes the bound. Likewise, a Z logical has odd parity in
all `r` rows and has weight exactly `r`. The
[dressed-distance proof](pedagogy/dressed-distance-and-decoding.md) makes the
quotient and the lower bounds explicit.

**6. Read two repetition syndromes.** Modulo horizontal Z gauge edges, a Z
error is completely specified by one parity bit per row. An X center strip
between rows `i` and `i+1` reports the XOR of the two adjacent row parities.
That is the open repetition-check matrix of length `r`. X errors reduce to
column parities and the length-`c` repetition check in the other direction.
Perfect-syndrome decoding is therefore two classical decisions; noisy gauge
extraction is a spacetime inference problem.

**7. Gauge-fix without confusing logical names.** On the `3 × 3` member,
promote all six horizontal `ZZ` gauge pairs to stabilizers and retain the two
X center strips. Their row space equals the repository's nine-qubit Shor
stabilizer row space. The neighboring Shor entry chooses encoded-basis names
in which its logical X is the Z column and its logical Z is the X row, the
reverse of this card's Pauli-type labels. The
[operation and gauge-fixing page](pedagogy/operations-gauge-fixing-and-variants.md)
records both the exact row-space equality and this logical-basis dictionary.

## Multiple pictures

- **Gauge group, center, quotient.** `G` is nonabelian, `S=Z(G)` fixes the
  codespace, and protected Paulis live in the centralizer of `S` modulo `G`.
  This is the executable picture used by `constructor.py`.

- **Two repetition codes.** Z errors collapse to row parities and X errors to
  column parities. Center syndromes are adjacent parity differences. This is
  the shortest decoding picture and explains why stretching the rectangle
  changes the two distances in opposite directions.

- **Compass Hamiltonian.** Reading the same pair generators as Hamiltonian
  terms produces alternating XX/ZZ compass interactions and rigid line
  symmetries. The dictionary exposes the center but does not make the ordinary
  static model a topological or self-correcting memory.

- **Gauge-fixed Shor block.** Choosing a commuting set of horizontal ZZ gauge
  edges removes gauge freedom and recovers the nine-qubit Shor stabilizer
  space. Gauge fixing changes which observables are fixed; it is not deletion
  of qubits or proof that all subsystem and subspace conventions coincide.

- **Tensor-leg reassignment.** A surface-code tensor network can expose
  selected legs as logical rather than physical, yielding the Bacon–Shor
  gauge bookkeeping. This is a representation dictionary, not an exact
  check-matrix replay adapter in the present repository.

- **Frustration graph and dynamical descendant.** The gauge anticommutation
  graph records which perpendicular pair terms meet once. A period-four
  Floquet–Bacon–Shor schedule turns related local measurements into
  time-dependent detectors and logical representatives; it is a different
  spacetime object, not another rendering of this static center.

The [representations and realizations ledger](pedagogy/representations-and-realizations.md)
states the equivalences and non-equivalences. The guided
[gauge-to-center tour](../../tours/bacon_shor.html) lets the reader inspect the
exact pair edges, center strips, bare logicals, gauge fix, and rectangular
counterfactual from constructor data.

## Why these parameters

**Why `n=rc`.** The rectangle has one physical qubit per site and no boundary
identifications or deleted sites.

**Why only one protected qubit.** The local gauge span has rank
`2rc-r-c`; its center has rank `r+c-2`. Substituting those two independently
recomputed ranks into the subsystem dimension formula leaves `k=1` for every
`r,c >= 2`. The remaining `(r-1)(c-1)` encoded degrees of freedom are gauge
qubits, not extra protected logicals.

**Why the distances follow the opposite dimension.** An X-type dressed
logical must carry odd parity in each column and therefore occupies at least
`c` sites; a complete row attains that weight. A Z-type dressed logical must
carry odd parity in each row and therefore has weight `r`; a complete column
attains it. The scalar distance is the smaller sector.

**Why the square members look symmetric.** For `r=c=L`, X and Z distances
both equal `L`, while the gauge count becomes `(L-1)^2`. Symmetry exchanges X
and Z only after transposing the grid; physical Hadamards without that
permutation do not restore the declared orientation.

**Why the `3 × 5` member is useful.** Its X logical crosses five columns
while its Z logical crosses three rows. Aspect ratio can therefore match a
noise bias, but the optimal rectangle also depends on physical error rates,
extraction circuits, objective, and operation costs. It is not a code-only
constant.

`instances.yaml` marks `n`, `k`, and CSS status `verified`. Distances and gauge
counts remain structured literature claims because the shared verifier has no
subsystem quotient implementation; `pedagogy/reproduce.py` supplies an
entry-specific independent audit without silently upgrading their provenance.

## Failure modes

- **Treating every gauge generator as a stabilizer.** A vertical `XX` and an
  incident horizontal `ZZ` anticommute. Requiring simultaneous `+1`
  eigenvalues would define no common stabilizer subspace. Only center products
  are stabilizers.

- **Counting `n-rank(S)` protected qubits.** That expression also counts the
  disposable gauge subsystem. The protected count uses both `rank(G)` and
  `rank(S)`; the `3 × 3` block has one protected qubit and four gauge qubits,
  not five protected qubits.

- **Confusing bare and dressed logicals.** A bare logical commutes with every
  gauge generator and appears as a complete row or column. A dressed logical
  need only commute with the center; gauge multiplication can bend it to one
  occupied site per column or row. Distance minimizes dressed weight.

- **Calling local gauge checks local stabilizers.** The measured factors have
  weight two, but their center products span complete strips whose weight
  grows with the perpendicular block dimension.

- **Multiplying outcomes from incompatible times without a circuit model.**
  Noncommuting X- and Z-gauge measurements disturb one another's raw values.
  A persistent detector requires an ordered schedule, repeated outcomes, and
  a convention for which products are compared across rounds.

- **Importing a threshold from a different protocol.** Static perfect gauge
  readout, repeated noisy pair extraction, encoded-ancilla Steane extraction,
  self-concatenated surgery, and period-four Floquet detectors expose
  different syndrome objects. As of the 2026-08-02 decoder sweep, no
  extraction-independent threshold for unspecified static Bacon–Shor
  stabilizer products was found.

- **Equating gauge fixing with an identity of logical labels.** The square
  gauge fix reproduces the Shor stabilizer row space, but this entry and the
  Shor entry choose opposite encoded-basis names for the X-row/Z-column pair.
  The algebra is the same only after that dictionary is stated.

## Operations story

**Pairwise CNOT.** Apply one physical CNOT between corresponding sites of two
equally shaped blocks. An X gauge on the control maps to the product of the
matching X gauges on control and target; a Z gauge on the target maps to the
matching pair on both blocks. The other two gauge types stay in their own
blocks. The gauge group and its center are preserved, and the row-X/column-Z
logical pair undergoes logical CNOT. Routing, extraction, and recovery are
additional resources.

**Hadamard on a square.** Physical H swaps X and Z, turning vertical X edges
into vertical Z edges and horizontal Z edges into horizontal X edges. A row/
column transposition then restores the declared gauge orientation and swaps
the logical row and column. The permutation is part of the gate.

**Gauge fixing.** Measuring and fixing the horizontal Z gauge edges on the
`3 × 3` block yields the Shor stabilizer presentation. More general choices
produce compass-code descendants. Which gauges are promoted, how their
outcomes set the Pauli frame, and how faults are handled are operation data,
not consequences of the word "gauge fix."

**Geometry-assisted non-Clifford routes.** Dimension-matched rectangular
blocks support cited transversal multi-controlled-Z constructions, while
biased-noise architectures combine strong aspect ratios with teleportation
and verified ancillas. Subsystem lattice surgery consumes compatible
boundaries and repeated joint measurements. Measurement-free deformation
replaces mid-circuit measurement with coherent correction and extra qubits.
The [operations ledger](pedagogy/operations-gauge-fixing-and-variants.md)
separates these mechanisms and their resource boundaries.

**Dynamical descendant.** Floquet–Bacon–Shor logical operations require a
period-four schedule, time-dependent logical tracking, detector decoding, and
feed-forward. They are evidence for the descendant named in the card, not
verified operations of the static check matrix exported here.

## Litmus questions

**Q1:** Why may two Bacon–Shor gauge generators anticommute? **A:** Gauge
outcomes describe an unprotected subsystem and need not be simultaneous
stabilizer eigenvalues. The protected subspace is fixed by center elements,
which commute with the whole gauge group.

**Q2:** How does a product of anticommuting local checks become a commuting
stabilizer? **A:** Multiply every parallel pair check across a complete gap.
Any perpendicular gauge edge then intersects the product on zero or two
qubits, so the total symplectic overlap is even.

**Q3:** Why does a `3 × 5` block have `d_X=5` and `d_Z=3` in this convention?
**A:** X gauge motion preserves one parity per column, so a nontrivial X
logical needs one occupied site in all five columns. Z gauge motion preserves
one parity per row, so a nontrivial Z logical needs one site in all three rows.

**Q4:** If the `3 × 3` center has four stabilizers, why is `k` not five?
**A:** Four additional encoded degrees of freedom are gauge qubits. Using
`rank(G)=12` and `rank(S)=4` gives
`k=9-(12+4)/2=1` and `g=(12-4)/2=4`.

**Q5:** What information does perfect Z-error decoding actually use? **A:**
Horizontal Z gauge motion erases all detail except each row's error parity.
The two X center syndromes on a three-row block report adjacent differences of
those three bits, exactly the classical repetition syndrome.

**Q6:** Does gauge-fixing Bacon–Shor to Shor preserve the names logical X and
logical Z used by both entry cards? **A:** It preserves the protected Pauli
algebra and exactly reproduces the Shor stabilizer row space, but the Shor
entry's encoded-basis convention calls the Z column logical X and the X row
logical Z. The labels are swapped relative to this card's Pauli-type names.

- **Frustration graph and dynamical descendant.** The gauge anticommutation
  graph records which perpendicular pair terms meet once. A period-four
  Floquet–Bacon–Shor schedule turns related local measurements into
  time-dependent detectors and logical representatives; it is a different
  spacetime object, not another rendering of this static center.

The [representations and realizations ledger](pedagogy/representations-and-realizations.md)
states the equivalences and non-equivalences. The guided
[gauge-to-center tour](../../tours/bacon_shor.html) lets the reader inspect the
exact pair edges, center strips, bare logicals, gauge fix, and rectangular
counterfactual from constructor data.

## Why these parameters

**Why `n=rc`.** The rectangle has one physical qubit per site and no boundary
identifications or deleted sites.

**Why only one protected qubit.** The local gauge span has rank
`2rc-r-c`; its center has rank `r+c-2`. Substituting those two independently
recomputed ranks into the subsystem dimension formula leaves `k=1` for every
`r,c >= 2`. The remaining `(r-1)(c-1)` encoded degrees of freedom are gauge
qubits, not extra protected logicals.

**Why the distances follow the opposite dimension.** An X-type dressed
logical must carry odd parity in each column and therefore occupies at least
`c` sites; a complete row attains that weight. A Z-type dressed logical must
carry odd parity in each row and therefore has weight `r`; a complete column
attains it. The scalar distance is the smaller sector.

**Why the square members look symmetric.** For `r=c=L`, X and Z distances
both equal `L`, while the gauge count becomes `(L-1)^2`. Symmetry exchanges X
and Z only after transposing the grid; physical Hadamards without that
permutation do not restore the declared orientation.

**Why the `3 × 5` member is useful.** Its X logical crosses five columns
while its Z logical crosses three rows. Aspect ratio can therefore match a
noise bias, but the optimal rectangle also depends on physical error rates,
extraction circuits, objective, and operation costs. It is not a code-only
constant.

`instances.yaml` marks `n`, `k`, and CSS status `verified`. Distances and gauge
counts remain structured literature claims because the shared verifier has no
subsystem quotient implementation; `pedagogy/reproduce.py` supplies an
entry-specific independent audit without silently upgrading their provenance.

## Failure modes

- **Treating every gauge generator as a stabilizer.** A vertical `XX` and an
  incident horizontal `ZZ` anticommute. Requiring simultaneous `+1`
  eigenvalues would define no common stabilizer subspace. Only center products
  are stabilizers.

- **Counting `n-rank(S)` protected qubits.** That expression also counts the
  disposable gauge subsystem. The protected count uses both `rank(G)` and
  `rank(S)`; the `3 × 3` block has one protected qubit and four gauge qubits,
  not five protected qubits.

- **Confusing bare and dressed logicals.** A bare logical commutes with every
  gauge generator and appears as a complete row or column. A dressed logical
  need only commute with the center; gauge multiplication can bend it to one
  occupied site per column or row. Distance minimizes dressed weight.

- **Calling local gauge checks local stabilizers.** The measured factors have
  weight two, but their center products span complete strips whose weight
  grows with the perpendicular block dimension.

- **Multiplying outcomes from incompatible times without a circuit model.**
  Noncommuting X- and Z-gauge measurements disturb one another's raw values.
  A persistent detector requires an ordered schedule, repeated outcomes, and
  a convention for which products are compared across rounds.

- **Importing a threshold from a different protocol.** Static perfect gauge
  readout, repeated noisy pair extraction, encoded-ancilla Steane extraction,
  self-concatenated surgery, and period-four Floquet detectors expose
  different syndrome objects. As of the 2026-08-02 decoder sweep, no
  extraction-independent threshold for unspecified static Bacon–Shor
  stabilizer products was found.

- **Equating gauge fixing with an identity of logical labels.** The square
  gauge fix reproduces the Shor stabilizer row space, but this entry and the
  Shor entry choose opposite encoded-basis names for the X-row/Z-column pair.
  The algebra is the same only after that dictionary is stated.

## Operations story

**Pairwise CNOT.** Apply one physical CNOT between corresponding sites of two
equally shaped blocks. An X gauge on the control maps to the product of the
matching X gauges on control and target; a Z gauge on the target maps to the
matching pair on both blocks. The other two gauge types stay in their own
blocks. The gauge group and its center are preserved, and the row-X/column-Z
logical pair undergoes logical CNOT. Routing, extraction, and recovery are
additional resources.

**Hadamard on a square.** Physical H swaps X and Z, turning vertical X edges
into vertical Z edges and horizontal Z edges into horizontal X edges. A row/
column transposition then restores the declared gauge orientation and swaps
the logical row and column. The permutation is part of the gate.

**Gauge fixing.** Measuring and fixing the horizontal Z gauge edges on the
`3 × 3` block yields the Shor stabilizer presentation. More general choices
produce compass-code descendants. Which gauges are promoted, how their
outcomes set the Pauli frame, and how faults are handled are operation data,
not consequences of the word "gauge fix."

**Geometry-assisted non-Clifford routes.** Dimension-matched rectangular
blocks support cited transversal multi-controlled-Z constructions, while
biased-noise architectures combine strong aspect ratios with teleportation
and verified ancillas. Subsystem lattice surgery consumes compatible
boundaries and repeated joint measurements. Measurement-free deformation
replaces mid-circuit measurement with coherent correction and extra qubits.
The [operations ledger](pedagogy/operations-gauge-fixing-and-variants.md)
separates these mechanisms and their resource boundaries.

**Dynamical descendant.** Floquet–Bacon–Shor logical operations require a
period-four schedule, time-dependent logical tracking, detector decoding, and
feed-forward. They are evidence for the descendant named in the card, not
verified operations of the static check matrix exported here.

## Litmus questions

**Q1:** Why may two Bacon–Shor gauge generators anticommute? **A:** Gauge
outcomes describe an unprotected subsystem and need not be simultaneous
stabilizer eigenvalues. The protected subspace is fixed by center elements,
which commute with the whole gauge group.

**Q2:** How does a product of anticommuting local checks become a commuting
stabilizer? **A:** Multiply every parallel pair check across a complete gap.
Any perpendicular gauge edge then intersects the product on zero or two
qubits, so the total symplectic overlap is even.

**Q3:** Why does a `3 × 5` block have `d_X=5` and `d_Z=3` in this convention?
**A:** X gauge motion preserves one parity per column, so a nontrivial X
logical needs one occupied site in all five columns. Z gauge motion preserves
one parity per row, so a nontrivial Z logical needs one site in all three rows.

**Q4:** If the `3 × 3` center has four stabilizers, why is `k` not five?
**A:** Four additional encoded degrees of freedom are gauge qubits. Using
`rank(G)=12` and `rank(S)=4` gives
`k=9-(12+4)/2=1` and `g=(12-4)/2=4`.

**Q5:** What information does perfect Z-error decoding actually use? **A:**
Horizontal Z gauge motion erases all detail except each row's error parity.
The two X center syndromes on a three-row block report adjacent differences of
those three bits, exactly the classical repetition syndrome.

**Q6:** Does gauge-fixing Bacon–Shor to Shor preserve the names logical X and
logical Z used by both entry cards? **A:** It preserves the protected Pauli
algebra and exactly reproduces the Shor stabilizer row space, but the Shor
entry's encoded-basis convention calls the Z column logical X and the X row
logical Z. The labels are swapped relative to this card's Pauli-type names.

documents.markdown:
# Bacon–Shor — Level-2 map

The phrase "local subsystem repetition code" compresses several different
statements. These pages separate the algebra that is recomputed from the
protocol claims that remain tied to literature.

1. [Gauge group, center, and subsystem qubit count](gauge-center-and-qubits.md):
   the declared orientation, pair-generator ranks, strip stabilizers,
   noncommutation, center containment, protected-qubit count, and gauge-qubit
   count.
2. [Dressed distance and the two repetition decoders](dressed-distance-and-decoding.md):
   row/column parity quotients, exact sector lower bounds and witnesses,
   bare-versus-dressed representatives, and worked perfect-syndrome tables.
3. [Gauge measurement and fault-tolerance boundaries](measurement-and-fault-tolerance.md):
   reconstructing center outcomes from pair measurements, why time order is
   decoder data, and why static, encoded-ancilla, concatenated, and Floquet
   performance claims cannot be merged.
4. [Operations, gauge fixing, and variants](operations-gauge-fixing-and-variants.md):
   pairwise CNOT, square-block Hadamard with transposition, exact Shor
   row-space recovery with the logical-label dictionary, and the resources
   consumed by cited non-Clifford and surgery mechanisms.
5. [Representation and realization ledger](representations-and-realizations.md):
   compass, tensor, frustration-graph, autonomous, and Floquet dictionaries;
   static trapped-ion versus dynamical superconducting evidence; and explicit
   non-equivalences.

## Reproduction contract

Run from the repository root:

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
python atlas/bacon_shor/pedagogy/reproduce.py
make verify-entry E=atlas/bacon_shor
```

`reproduce.py` builds all three shipped rectangles and independently derives
their gauge and center support matrices. It asserts generator counts and
ranks, center containment, noncommuting local pairs, protected and gauge
dimensions, bare logical commutation, exact pure-X and pure-Z dressed
distances, repetition-syndrome factorization, pair-outcome reconstruction,
square-block Hadamard/transposition symmetry, the exact Shor gauge-fixed row
space and logical-label swap, scene/tour integrity, and T3 packet state.

The shared `qeclib.distance` API now minimizes physical Pauli weight in
`C(S)/G`: exact search finishes complete weight layers and the verifier
recomputes the three shipped finite `d` claims. The committed evidence rows
also retain one seeded `5 × 7` witness of achieved weight `12` as
`bounded`, with method `rand-subsystem-dressed-logical-coset-v1`, seed `17`,
and `not-certified` optimality. The independent witness gate checks
stabilizer commutation, gauge nontriviality, and physical weight. This row is
not a lower bound, an exact distance, or evidence for the family formula.

The card also omits a `construction:` tree. No registered operation adapter
currently expresses the rectangular pair-gauge construction with exact row
and qubit order. The deterministic constructor and this transcript establish
the shipped presentation without pretending that an unsupported generic
replay exists. The broader problem of certifying equality across gauge-fixed,
subsystem, and subspace presentations is tracked by
`wanted:code-equivalence`; the exact square-to-Shor row-space witness on this
entry is evidence for one pair, not a general canonicalizer.

## Provenance split

- **Recomputed facts:** qubit order; local gauge and center supports; all
  finite-instance ranks; center/gauge containment; `n=rc`, `k=1`, and
  `(r-1)(c-1)` gauge qubits; bare logical row/column algebra; exact pure-sector
  dressed distances for the shipped rectangles; repetition quotient and
  single-error syndrome tables; center-outcome products; square
  Hadamard/transposition mapping; exact `3 × 3` gauge-fixed Shor stabilizer
  row space and the cross-entry logical-label dictionary; constructor-derived
  scene and tour data.
- **Bounded facts:** the committed `5 × 7`, seed-`17`, `32`-trial search
  achieves a weight-`12` dressed-logical representative and independently
  validates it. Its only guarantee is an upper bound; optimality is explicitly
  `not-certified`.
- **Literature claims:** historical subsystem construction; fault-tolerant
  extraction and decoder behavior beyond perfect gauge outcomes; biased-noise
  optimization; thresholds or logical rates of named circuits; transversal
  controlled-phase families; surgery, teleportation, deformation, and
  autonomous-dynamics resources; compass, tensor, and frustration-graph
  dictionaries; and every hardware demonstration.

No threshold, pseudo-threshold, one-point logical error rate, or device error
rate is quoted in this packet. Dated negative findings are retained at the
reader-facing location where they are used.

documents.title: Dressed distance and the two repetition decoders
documents.markdown:
# Dressed distance and the two repetition decoders

The same parity quotient proves both the sector distances and the
perfect-gauge-readout decoder. This page fixes the meaning of "modulo gauge"
before using a repetition analogy.

## X-type dressed operators

Represent an X-type Pauli by a binary `r × c` support matrix `A`. Multiplying
by a vertical X gauge edge flips two adjacent entries in one column. Such
moves preserve the column-parity vector

$$p_j=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}A_{i,j}\pmod 2.$$

Conversely, adjacent-pair moves generate every even-parity pattern inside a
column. Two X supports are therefore in the same X-gauge coset exactly when
they have the same `c` column parities.

Commutation with the Z center strip between columns `j` and `j+1` requires

$$p_j+p_{j+1}=0.$$

All column parities of a dressed X normalizer must be equal. The all-zero
choice is X-gauge-trivial. The only nontrivial protected choice is

$$p=(1,1,\ldots,1).$$

Any support in this coset contains at least one X in every column, so its
weight is at least `c`. A complete X row has exactly one occupied site per
column and realizes the bound:

$$d_X=c.$$

The row is bare, but a general minimum representative can zig-zag by
multiplying vertical gauge edges. This is the concrete difference between a
bare logical and a dressed logical.

## Z-type dressed operators

For a Z support matrix `B`, horizontal Z gauge edges generate every
even-parity pattern within a row. The gauge invariant is the row-parity vector

$$u_i=\sum_{j=0}^{c-1}B_{i,j}\pmod 2.$$

Commutation with adjacent-row X center strips forces every `u_i` to be equal.
The zero vector is gauge-trivial; the nontrivial protected coset has one in
every row. At least one Z is needed per row, and a complete column reaches the
bound:

$$d_Z=r.$$

For a CSS subsystem code with this single protected pair, a mixed Pauli cannot
beat both pure-sector minima: its X and Z support components must each be
either gauge-trivial or in the corresponding logical parity class, and its
Pauli weight contains the support of every nontrivial component. Hence

$$d=\min(r,c).$$

`reproduce.py` exhausts all pure-X and pure-Z supports through these minima
for every shipped rectangle and checks nonmembership in the full gauge row
space. Independently, the shared referee enumerates mixed Pauli supports in
increasing weight and verifies the total `d` values `2`, `3`, and `3` for the
shipped `2 × 2`, `3 × 3`, and `3 × 5` instances. The structured total-distance
claims therefore carry `verified` origins. The `d_X` and `d_Z` rows remain
literature-attributed because the generic referee reports the minimum over all
Pauli types rather than two named sectors.

The exact enumerator refuses an over-budget layer before treating partial
work as a lower bound. For the committed `5 × 7` case, the separate seeded
search finds a weight-`12` representative in `32` trials with seed `17`; the
independent validator accepts the Pauli, while the evidence envelope records
`optimality: not-certified`. This is an achieved upper bound only and does not
replace the parity proof of the rectangular family formula.

## Z errors become a repetition problem on rows

Let `E` be a Z-error support and retain only its row parities `u`. Horizontal
Z gauge motion changes positions within a row without changing `u`. The
X-center syndrome between rows `i` and `i+1` is

$$s^X_i=u_i+u_{i+1}.$$

Thus the protected syndrome is exactly the open repetition parity matrix
applied to `u`. There are two row-parity patterns for a given syndrome; they
differ by the all-one vector. That difference is the logical Z coset. Under a
specified independent-noise prior, the decoder chooses between those two
cosets by likelihood or majority logic.

For the `3 × 3` block, one Z error in each possible row gives:

| representative | row parity `u` | X-center syndrome `(s0,s1)` |
|---|---|---|
| `Z` on `q0` | `100` | `10` |
| `Z` on `q3` | `010` | `11` |
| `Z` on `q6` | `001` | `01` |

The column position is absent because changing it by horizontal Z gauge edges
does not change the protected action.

If physical Z errors are independent with probability `p`, the probability
that one row of length `c` has odd parity is

$$p_{row}=\sum_{w\text{ odd}}{c\choose w}p^w(1-p)^{c-w}
=\frac{1-(1-2p)^c}{2}.$$

This formula defines the perfect-readout effective repetition channel. It is
not a circuit-level threshold: measurement faults, propagation, correlations,
and repeated-round inference are absent.

## X errors become a repetition problem on columns

The perpendicular argument retains one parity `p_j` for each column. The
Z-center syndrome is

$$s^Z_j=p_j+p_{j+1}.$$

On the `3 × 3` block:

| representative | column parity `p` | Z-center syndrome `(s0,s1)` |
|---|---|---|
| `X` on `q0` | `100` | `10` |
| `X` on `q1` | `010` | `11` |
| `X` on `q2` | `001` | `01` |

For independent X errors with probability `p`, the odd parity of a column of
height `r` has probability `[1-(1-2p)^r]/2`. A `3 × 5` rectangle therefore
creates a length-five column-parity repetition decision for X errors and a
length-three row-parity decision for Z errors. Which shape is optimal depends
on both physical channels and the complete correction protocol.

## Degeneracy is the algorithm, not a nuisance

An ordinary decoder might try to identify the exact physical error. Here that
goal is unnecessarily strict. All supports with the same row or column parity
differ by gauge action and are equivalent on the protected subsystem. The
minimal sufficient statistic for perfect readout is the parity vector, and
the only remaining ambiguity is whether it belongs to the trivial or logical
all-one coset.

This quotient is also why a stabilizer-only distance routine is wrong for the
entry. Quotienting only by `S` would retain many operators that differ by
noncentral gauge action and would misclassify disposable degrees of freedom as
protected logicals.

## Boundary of the perfect-syndrome result

The tables above assume exact center syndromes. In a hardware circuit one
normally measures weight-two gauge generators, not the strips directly. Raw
gauge outcomes from different Pauli rounds can be disturbed, and a faulty
ancilla interaction can change both data and measurement records. The decoder
must consume the actual schedule's history. The next page derives the safe
outcome products and then separates the named circuit-level regimes:
[gauge measurement and fault tolerance](measurement-and-fault-tolerance.md).

documents.title: Gauge group, center, and subsystem qubit count
documents.markdown:
# Gauge group, center, and subsystem qubit count

This page derives the static rectangular presentation exported by
`constructor.py`. It uses sign-free Pauli algebra; phases do not enter any
rank or commutation statement.

## Coordinate and Pauli convention

Let rows be indexed by `i=0,...,r-1` and columns by `j=0,...,c-1`. The
row-major qubit index is

$$q(i,j)=ic+j.$$

The local gauge generators are

$$g^X_{i,j}=X_{i,j}X_{i+1,j},\qquad
0\le i<r-1,\ 0\le j<c,$$

and

$$g^Z_{i,j}=Z_{i,j}Z_{i,j+1},\qquad
0\le i<r,\ 0\le j<c-1.$$

Thus X edges are vertical and Z edges are horizontal. The convention is
deliberate: it makes a bare X logical span a row and a bare Z logical span a
column. Transposing the grid and exchanging X/Z is equivalent, but it swaps
the sector labels used below.

## Why the gauge group is nonabelian

Two generators of the same Pauli type commute. A vertical X edge and a
horizontal Z edge anticommute exactly when they share one endpoint. For the
`3 × 3` constructor order,

`g^X_{0,0}=X_0X_3`

and

`g^Z_{0,0}=Z_0Z_1`

share only `q0`, so their symplectic product is one. The tour highlights this
pair as gauge items zero and six. This is why the individual pair outcomes
cannot all be stabilizer eigenvalues.

## Constructing the center

For each adjacent row pair, multiply every vertical X edge across the columns:

$$S^X_i=\prod_{j=0}^{c-1}g^X_{i,j}
=\prod_{j=0}^{c-1}X_{i,j}X_{i+1,j}.$$

For each adjacent column pair, multiply every horizontal Z edge across the
rows:

$$S^Z_j=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}g^Z_{i,j}
=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}Z_{i,j}Z_{i,j+1}.$$

An X strip and a Z strip overlap on the four corners of their `2 × 2`
intersection, so they commute. More strongly, an X strip meets an individual
horizontal Z edge on zero or two sites, and a Z strip meets an individual
vertical X edge on zero or two sites. Every strip therefore commutes with the
entire gauge group, not merely with the other strips.

The constructor checks both statements:

- `CheckMatrix.validate()` rejects any stabilizer/gauge anticommutation;
- `rank([G;S])=rank(G)` proves that every declared center row lies in the
  generated gauge span.

## Rank ledger

Within one column, the vertical X supports are the `r-1` rows of the open
length-`r` repetition parity matrix. They are independent. Different columns
have disjoint supports, so

$$rank(G_X)=c(r-1).$$

Similarly, the horizontal Z supports form an independent length-`c` open
chain inside each row:

$$rank(G_Z)=r(c-1).$$

X-only and Z-only symplectic rows occupy different binary halves, so their
ranks add:

$$rank(G)=c(r-1)+r(c-1)=2rc-r-c.$$

The X center contains `r-1` independent adjacent-row strips; the Z center
contains `c-1` independent adjacent-column strips. Hence

$$rank(S)=r+c-2.$$

For a subsystem code with gauge group `G` and center stabilizer group `S`, the
protected and gauge dimensions are

$$k=n-\frac{rank(G)+rank(S)}{2},\qquad
g=\frac{rank(G)-rank(S)}{2}.$$

Substituting `n=rc` gives

$$k=1,\qquad g=rc-r-c+1=(r-1)(c-1).$$

The three shipped instances therefore have the following independently
recomputed ledger:

| rectangle | `rank(S)` | `rank(G)` | protected `k` | gauge `g` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `2 × 2` | 2 | 4 | 1 | 1 |
| `3 × 3` | 4 | 12 | 1 | 4 |
| `3 × 5` | 6 | 22 | 1 | 8 |

The structured gauge-count claims cite the subsystem literature because the
ordinary entry verifier exposes `k` but does not emit gauge-qubit claims.
`reproduce.py` checks every table cell without changing that provenance class.

## Bare protected Pauli algebra

Choose

$$\bar X_b=\prod_{j=0}^{c-1}X_{0,j},\qquad
\bar Z_b=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}Z_{i,0}.$$

The subscript `b` means *bare*: each operator commutes with the full gauge
group. `\bar X_b` meets each horizontal Z edge in its row twice, and
`\bar Z_b` meets each vertical X edge in its column twice. They meet each
other once at `q(0,0)`, so they anticommute and generate one protected Pauli
pair.

A complete X row at height `i` differs from the row at `i+1` by `S^X_i`.
Likewise, neighboring complete Z columns differ by `S^Z_j`. Parallel bare
representatives therefore differ by center elements, which are also gauge
elements.

This bare pair proves a protected qubit exists, but it is not yet the distance
proof. Distance permits multiplication by noncentral gauge operators and thus
minimizes over dressed representatives; that quotient is derived on the
[distance page](dressed-distance-and-decoding.md).

## What the calculation does not establish

- It does not specify a measurement schedule. Noncommuting pair generators
  require time ordering and a detector convention.
- It does not turn the long center strips into local stabilizers. Only their
  measurement factors are local.
- It does not prove a scalable distance theorem merely because the shared
  Atlas referee exactly enumerates the shipped small instances. Certified
  lower bounds beyond the exact-search ceiling and equivalence-safe changes
  of subsystem presentation remain routed to
  `wanted:subsystem-dressed-distance`.
- It does not make the compass Hamiltonian self-correcting or topological.
  Hamiltonian protection is a dynamics claim with separate evidence.

documents.title: Gauge measurement and fault-tolerance boundaries
documents.markdown:
# Gauge measurement and fault-tolerance boundaries

The algebra says a center strip is a product of local gauge generators. A
fault-tolerant protocol must additionally say when those factors are measured,
which outcomes are multiplied, how measurement faults are detected, and what
history reaches the decoder.

## Reconstructing one center outcome

All X-type gauge generators commute with one another. In an X-gauge round,
measure the `c` vertical pairs crossing a fixed adjacent-row gap and record
outcomes `m^X_{i,j}` in `{+1,-1}`. Their product is the eigenvalue of the
X-center strip:

$$\sigma^X_i=\prod_{j=0}^{c-1}m^X_{i,j}.$$

Likewise, in a Z-gauge round the product of the `r` horizontal-pair outcomes
across one adjacent-column gap gives

$$\sigma^Z_j=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}m^Z_{i,j}.$$

`reproduce.py` verifies the operator identities by XORing the corresponding
symplectic gauge rows and comparing the exact constructor stabilizer rows.
This proves the noiseless product rule. It does not certify a measurement
circuit.

## Why raw gauge outcomes are not persistent syndrome bits

An X gauge edge and a Z gauge edge that meet once anticommute. Measuring the Z
edge after the X edge may randomize the earlier X gauge eigenvalue. The center
product survives because it commutes with every gauge generator, but the
individual factor history depends on time order.

A circuit-level detector therefore needs at least:

1. an ordered X/Z gauge schedule;
2. a convention identifying which same-type outcomes form one center sample;
3. repeated samples or other redundancy for measurement faults;
4. data-error propagation rules for each ancilla interaction;
5. a decoder mapping the resulting spacetime record to a protected logical
   correction modulo gauge.

Multiplying one X-round outcome with a later Z-round outcome has no
schedule-independent meaning. Even comparing the same gauge factor at two
times is safe only after the intervening measurements and detector convention
are specified.

## Four decoder inputs that must not be conflated

| regime | data presented to the decoder | statement licensed |
|---|---|---|
| perfect static gauge readout | exact center parities derived from exact pair outcomes | two finite classical repetition decisions modulo gauge |
| repeated low-weight extraction | a time history of pair outcomes, repetitions, and possibly flags | performance of that named extraction circuit and recovery rule |
| encoded-ancilla Steane extraction | encoded-ancilla verification plus blockwise extraction outcomes | comparison with other complete ancilla/extraction protocols |
| period-four Floquet descendant | constant-weight spacetime detectors from the scheduled dynamical code | performance and logical behavior of the descendant, not the static center |

The first row is derived on the
[distance/decoding page](dressed-distance-and-decoding.md). The other rows are
literature claims because their circuit, noise, and postprocessing layers are
not exported by this static constructor.

## Repeated pair extraction

Low gauge weight limits how many data qubits one ancilla interaction chain
touches, but "weight two" is not itself fault tolerance. A fault can occur on
the ancilla, a two-qubit gate, preparation, measurement, idling data, or a
classical record. Repeating gauge measurements supplies time redundancy, and
the decoder must infer a protected center history despite local gauge values
that may legitimately change.

Cross, DiVincenzo, and Terhal (`cross2009comparative`) provide the fixed-block
repeated-syndrome/majority baseline. Its performance belongs to the complete
small-block circuit and stochastic model. It is not a universal property of
the `3 × 3` check matrix.

## Encoded-ancilla extraction

Steane-style extraction couples an encoded ancilla block transversally rather
than measuring every gauge pair with an individual bare ancilla. The ancilla
preparation, verification, coupling direction, measured block, accepted
histories, and recovery rule define a different syndrome object.

Escobar-Arrieta and Gutiérrez (`escobar2025improved`) compare this route with a
Shor-style extraction protocol. The comparison cannot be transferred to an
unspecified "Bacon–Shor decoder" because changing extraction changes both the
fault locations and the available side information.

## Self-concatenated surgery and Floquet detectors

`gidney2023less` obtains threshold behavior from local lattice-surgery
circuits arranged in a self-concatenating construction. The fitted family is
the circuit construction, not a direct sequence of increasingly large static
rectangles under an unspecified stabilizer measurement.

`alam2025board` instead defines a period-four measurement schedule with
constant-weight spacetime detectors and applies matching under a uniform
circuit-level model. Time-dependent checks and logical representatives are
part of that code definition. The scheduled descendant is therefore recorded
as an R3 view, not as a schedule exported by this static entry.

## Threshold identity boundary

This packet quotes no threshold-like number. Before any future number enters,
the full identity tuple must include:

1. static rectangle, concatenated circuit, or Floquet descendant;
2. scaling variable and fitted logical observable;
3. exact extraction circuit or measurement schedule;
4. noise model and normalization per location or round;
5. decoder, repetition/postselection rule, and version;
6. source figure, table, or section;
7. threshold, pseudo-threshold, one-point logical rate, bound, or hardware
   result.

The 2026-08-02 decoder sweep found no extraction-independent threshold for
plain unspecified static stabilizer products. That dated negative result does
not say no Bacon–Shor-derived protocol has a threshold; it says the protocol
identity cannot be erased.

## Source ledger

- `aliferis2007subsystem`: low-weight gauge extraction and subsystem
  fault-tolerant gadgets.
- `cross2009comparative`: repeated-syndrome fixed-block circuit baseline.
- `napp2013optimal`: perfect-readout biased-noise decoding and rectangle
  optimization, with model-dependent optima.
- `escobar2025improved`: complete encoded-ancilla versus Shor-style extraction
  comparison.
- `gidney2023less`: self-concatenated local-surgery threshold construction.
- `alam2025board`: scheduled period-four detectors and MWPM for the Floquet
  descendant.

Every bibkey resolves in `registry/refs.yaml`; the fetch-verification details
and dated searches are retained in `docs/lit/bacon_shor/`.

documents.title: Operations, gauge fixing, and variants
documents.markdown:
# Operations, gauge fixing, and variants

This page separates operations proved from the exported gauge algebra from
protocols whose fault tolerance and resource cost remain literature claims.

## Pairwise physical CNOT

Take two identically ordered `r × c` blocks, A as control and B as target,
and apply physical CNOT pairwise at every grid site. Pauli conjugation gives

$$X_A\mapsto X_AX_B,\quad X_B\mapsto X_B,$$

$$Z_A\mapsto Z_A,\quad Z_B\mapsto Z_AZ_B.$$

Apply these rules to each local generator:

- an X gauge edge in A maps to the matching X gauge edge in both A and B;
- an X gauge edge in B remains in B;
- a Z gauge edge in A remains in A;
- a Z gauge edge in B maps to the matching Z gauge edge in both blocks.

Every image is in the two-block gauge group, so the center and protected
subsystem are preserved. The bare logical row and column obey the same
conjugation rules, giving logical CNOT in this card's Pauli-type convention.
This establishes the abstract transversal layer. It does not include routing,
faulty CNOT locations, extraction, or recovery.

## Hadamard requires a square and a transpose

Physical H swaps X and Z. On the declared grid it maps vertical X gauge edges
to vertical Z edges and horizontal Z gauge edges to horizontal X edges, which
does not match `constructor.py`'s orientation. Transpose the grid coordinates
after the H layer:

`(i,j) -> (j,i)`.

Vertical edges become horizontal and horizontal edges become vertical. For a
square block this restores the gauge-generator set and exchanges the logical
X row with the logical Z column. A nonsquare rectangle is mapped to the
transposed `c × r` block, so it is not an unchanged-block transversal H.

`reproduce.py` performs this support map on the `3 × 3` generator set and
checks exact equality after the Pauli swap.

## Exact `3 × 3` gauge fix to the Shor stabilizer space

The square Bacon–Shor center contains two X strips:

`XXXXXX___` and `___XXXXXX`.

Promote all six horizontal Z gauge pairs to stabilizers:

`ZZ_______`, `_ZZ______`, `___ZZ____`, `____ZZ___`,
`______ZZ_`, and `_______ZZ`.

These eight rows are exactly the set exported by `atlas/shor_nine/`, up to row
order. The reproduction transcript loads both constructors and proves mutual
row-space containment and equal rank; this is stronger than comparing the
parameter label `[[9,1,3]]`.

### The logical-label dictionary

The stabilizer equality does not license silently copying logical names. This
entry uses Pauli-type labels:

| Bacon–Shor name | representative | Shor entry's encoded-basis name |
|---|---|---|
| logical X | `XXX______` | logical Z |
| logical Z | `Z__Z__Z__` | logical X |

Both pairs generate the same protected Pauli algebra and anticommute once.
The Shor entry names them by their action on Shor's chosen encoded cat-state
basis, while this entry names them by physical Pauli type. The gauge fix
preserves the protected algebra but the cross-entry dictionary includes a
logical Hadamard relabeling.

Promoting a gauge operator also fixes one formerly disposable degree of
freedom. A fault-tolerant gauge-fixing protocol must record the measured
outcomes, any repeated checks, and the Pauli-frame update; row-space equality
alone is not a circuit.

## Compass-code gauge fixes

The full rectangle promotes all horizontal Z gauges in the Shor specialization.
Other commuting promotion patterns produce two-dimensional compass-code
descendants (`li2019compass`). The selected pattern changes stabilizer weights,
exposed syndrome information, and decoding geometry. It cannot be represented
by changing only `rows` and `columns` on this card, so the relation target is a
separate pending family.

Bravyi–Bacon–Shor changes a different resource: a binary occupancy matrix
chooses which grid sites exist. Its encoded dimension and distances are
properties of row and column codes of that matrix. The full rectangular
family here is a special case; generalized rate claims do not flow backward
to this card.

## Cited non-Clifford and interface mechanisms

| mechanism | what changes or is consumed | claim boundary |
|---|---|---|
| dimension-matched transversal controlled-Z family | rectangle dimensions and correction between protocol pieces | `yoder2017universalbacon`; not a universal transversal set on one fixed square |
| biased-noise teleportation | strong aspect ratio, verified ancillas, teleportation measurements, correction | `brooks2013asymmetric`; geometry alone is not the architecture |
| subsystem lattice surgery | compatible boundaries, ancilla code patch, repeated joint gauge measurements, feed-forward | `nautrup2017interface`; not pairwise block transversality |
| measurement-free deformation | coherent correction circuitry and extra qubits replace mid-circuit measurement | `veroni2025measurementfree`; measurement-free is not correction-free |
| Floquet logical control | period-four schedule, detector decoding, time-dependent logical tracking | `sun2025floquetbacon`; descendant only |

As of the 2026-08-02 operations sweep, no fetched source supports a universal
transversal set on one unchanged square Bacon–Shor block. Universality in the
cited protocols uses aspect-ratio changes, teleportation, deformation,
concatenation, surgery, or error-correction steps between pieces.

## Static algebra versus fault-tolerant gadget

The CNOT and square-H support maps are exact statements about ideal Pauli
conjugation. Calling them fault tolerant additionally requires a fault set,
propagation analysis, extraction schedule, decoder, and recovery placement.
The remaining operations in the table are kept `claimed` on `card.yaml`
because their resource and fault-tolerance statements come from named
protocols rather than the static constructor.

documents.title: Representation and realization ledger
documents.markdown:
# Representation and realization ledger

Several literatures use the same row/column structure for different purposes.
This ledger states what each picture preserves and what it does not license.

## Representation dictionary

| picture | exact object retained | insight gained | boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| gauge-center quotient | symplectic gauge rows, center rows, protected quotient | why noncommuting local checks can protect one qubit | canonical executable view |
| perpendicular repetition | row and column parity quotients | sector distances, degeneracy, and perfect-readout decoding | does not define a noisy extraction circuit |
| quantum compass Hamiltonian | local XX/ZZ interaction pattern and line symmetries | center strips as rigid symmetries | does not make the static model topological or self-correcting |
| surface-tensor leg reassignment | tensor-network operator-pushing dictionary | how physical/logical leg bookkeeping exposes weight-two gauges | not an exact constructor replay or equality of stabilizer row order |
| frustration graph | pairwise anticommutation of gauge terms | which perpendicular links obstruct simultaneous gauge values | ordinary Bacon–Shor is the obstructed relative, not labeled free-fermion solvable |
| autonomous gauge dynamics | gauge interactions plus a chosen dissipative/control model | how the disposable subsystem affects dynamical correction | dynamics claim, not a new static code parameter |
| period-four Floquet descendant | scheduled measurement graph, detectors, time-dependent logicals | how related pair measurements define a dynamical qubit | not the static `CheckMatrix` rendered at landing |

The first two rows are recomputed. The other rows are curated dictionaries
with registered primary references.

## Compass Hamiltonian

Assign the pair operators as local Hamiltonian terms. The same vertical-X and
horizontal-Z pattern becomes the square quantum compass model. Products along
complete lines commute with the Hamiltonian and mirror the center-strip
symmetries. This makes the energetic role of gauge degrees of freedom visible.

It does not follow that local pair terms produce a topologically ordered or
self-correcting memory. `dorier2005compass`, `bacon2006operator`, and
`sarma2013gauge` discuss the interaction/symmetry and autonomous-dynamics
questions with their own model assumptions. The static code entry exports no
Hamiltonian gap, bath, lifetime, or thermal scaling claim.

## Tensor-leg reassignment

`cao2022quantumlego` obtains a Bacon–Shor description by reorganizing a
surface-code tensor network and declaring selected dangling legs logical
rather than physical. Operator pushing then exposes the pair-gauge structure.

This is a useful explanation of subsystem bookkeeping: changing which tensor
legs count as protected versus disposable can turn a stabilizer presentation
into a gauge presentation. It is not an exact operation-tree adapter in this
repository. A contraction or leg reassignment can also create a new code whose
parameters must be recomputed rather than inherited.

## Frustration graph and the free-fermion boundary

Build a graph whose vertices are gauge terms and whose edges connect
anticommuting pairs. For the rectangular compass pattern, a vertical X edge is
adjacent to each horizontal Z edge sharing exactly one endpoint. The graph is
constructor-derivable and exposes the nonabelian measurement conflicts.

`chapman2022freefermion` uses Bacon–Shor as the obstructed comparison when
constructing a related free-fermion subsystem model. The fetched source does
not establish that ordinary Bacon–Shor is itself free-fermion solvable. The
card therefore labels this view a boundary, not a free-fermion realization.

## Static and dynamical hardware evidence

| platform/result | code object | established | not established |
|---|---|---|---|
| thirteen-qubit trapped-ion processor (`egan2021fault`) | nine data qubits in a static Bacon–Shor logical block plus four ancillas | fault-tolerant preparation, measurement, corrected rotations, and stabilizer-extraction primitives on a fixed block | increasing-distance below-threshold memory scaling |
| superconducting processor (`sun2025floquetbacon`) | scheduled Floquet–Bacon–Shor descendant | operations on a time-dependent dynamical logical qubit | realization of this card's static center/checkmatrix experiment |
| bias-preserving teleportation architecture (`brooks2013asymmetric`) | proposed strongly rectangular blocks inside a larger protocol | architecture and resource analysis under biased elementary operations | hardware demonstration or a code-only optimum aspect ratio |

The static trapped-ion experiment is the direct realization attached to this
card. The superconducting result is recorded as descendant evidence because
its logical qubit and detectors depend on a schedule absent from the static
constructor.

As of the 2026-08-02 realization sweep, no increasing-distance below-threshold
Bacon–Shor hardware scaling demonstration was found. That dated negative
result does not diminish the demonstrated fixed-block primitive suite; it
prevents the two evidence levels from being merged.

## Variant invariants

Use the following test before transferring a claim:

- changing only `r` and `c` preserves the rectangular pair-gauge grammar but
  changes sector distances and gauge count;
- changing the occupancy matrix creates Bravyi–Bacon–Shor row/column codes and
  can change protected dimension;
- promoting a commuting gauge subset changes the stabilizer group and creates
  a compass-code or Shor gauge fix;
- adding a time schedule changes the detector graph and logical evolution;
- changing tensor leg roles supplies a representation map whose exact output
  still needs parameter verification.

Matching words such as "compass," "Bacon–Shor," or "subsystem" do not prove
these objects have interchangeable distances, thresholds, operations, or
hardware evidence.

## Source and negative-result ledger

- Gauge/compass/autonomous: `bacon2006operator`, `dorier2005compass`,
  `sarma2013gauge`.
- Tensor dictionary: `cao2022quantumlego`.
- Frustration/free-fermion boundary: `chapman2022freefermion`.
- Static hardware: `egan2021fault`.
- Floquet descendant: `alam2025board`, `sun2025floquetbacon`.
- Biased architecture: `brooks2013asymmetric`.

The 2026-08-02 representation sweep found no source calling the ordinary
two-dimensional compass Hamiltonian a self-correcting topological memory, and
no source making the base code free-fermion solvable. Bibliographic identity,
queries, and correction notes are retained in the six local literature files.
